o: Count non-empty subsequences with no three consecutive same-parity elements, modulo 10⁹+7. Example 1: [1,3,5] → all 7 non-empty subsequences except [1,3,5] → 6. Example 2: [2,3,4,2] → 15 non-empty minus [2,4,2] → 14. Track, for each parity, how many stable subsequences end with a run of exactly 1 or exactly 2 same-parity elements; a new element extends runs of the opposite parity freely, converts run-1 same-parity tails into run-2, and cannot extend run-2 same-parity tails.
k: DP state dp[p][r] = number of stable subsequences ending with parity p and trailing same-parity run length r ∈ {1, 2}.
New element of parity q: dp[q][1] += 1 + dp[1−q][0] + dp[1−q][1] (start fresh or extend opposite-parity tails); dp[q][2] += dp[q][0].
Answer is the sum of all four states — every counted subsequence is stable by construction.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear DP on (Parity, Run Length)
a.i: Process elements left to right keeping four counters. Appending element x of parity q to any stable subsequence keeps stability unless that subsequence ends with two q-parity elements. Copy old states (existing subsequences persist), add the singleton, and add legal extensions.
s: For each x with q = x mod 2: new_dp[q][1] = dp[q][1] + 1 + dp[1−q][0] + dp[1−q][1]; new_dp[q][2] = dp[q][2] + dp[q][0]; other states copied.
After all elements, return (Σ dp) mod 1e9+7.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def countStableSubsequences(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
        dp = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]  # dp[parity][runlen-1]
        for x in nums:
            p = x & 1
            ndp = [row[:] for row in dp]
            ndp[p][0] = (dp[p][0] + 1 + dp[1 - p][0] + dp[1 - p][1]) % MOD
            ndp[p][1] = (dp[p][1] + dp[p][0]) % MOD
            dp = ndp
        return (dp[0][0] + dp[0][1] + dp[1][0] + dp[1][1]) % MOD

a.i: Define f(i, p, r) = number of stable completions choosing from suffix i given the last taken element had parity p with run length r (or a 'no previous' sentinel). Each position offers skip or take (take illegal if it would create three same-parity in a row). Memoize over (i, p, r) — O(n) states.
s: f(i, p, r): if i = n return 1 (the empty completion counts the chosen subsequence once at the top level — instead count non-empty via a wrapper).
Option take x: allowed unless p == parity(x) and r == 2; recurse with updated run state.
Sum take-branches over all first picks, or use a sentinel start state.

c.python:
import sys
from functools import lru_cache
class Solution:
    def countStableSubsequences(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10 ** 9 + 7
        sys.setrecursionlimit(300000)
        n = len(nums)
        @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
        def f(i, p, r):
            if i == n: return 1
            res = f(i + 1, p, r)
            q = nums[i] & 1
            nr = (r + 1) if (p == q and r > 0) else 1
            if nr <= 2:
                res = (res + f(i + 1, q, nr)) % MOD
            return res
        return (f(0, 2, 0) - 1) % MOD  # subtract the empty subsequence

a.t: O(n) — each (i, parity, run) state solved once (sentinel p=2 covers 'no previous').
a.sp: O(n) for the memo table plus recursion stack.

w: The bottom-up four-counter DP is the model answer: O(n) time, O(1) space. Pitfalls: forgetting the '+1' for the singleton subsequence, accidentally extending run-2 same-parity tails (instability), and forgetting to subtract/exclude the empty subsequence in the top-down formulation. Follow-up: forbid runs of length m, or count subsequences avoiding an arbitrary pattern.
